scenario: You are writing a tool description for a send_email tool that can both draft and send emails. Claude keeps using it to send emails when users only want to draft them.
question: What is missing from this tool description?
options: The tool description must include WHAT it does, WHEN to use it, and explicitly WHEN NOT to use it (e.g., 'Do not use this tool to send an email if the user only asked to draft or preview it')
The tool needs a more creative name
The tool needs more parameters so Claude can infer intent better
The tool_choice should be set to 'auto' to give Claude full discretion
explanation: A complete tool description must include: (1) WHAT the tool does mechanically, (2) WHEN to use it (triggering conditions), and (3) WHEN NOT to use it (exclusion conditions). The third element is most commonly omitted and causes exactly the described problem — Claude uses a capable tool when it shouldn't. Adding an explicit 'Do not call this tool when the user only wants to draft or preview' rule eliminates the ambiguity. More parameters (C) and tool_choice auto (D) won't help if the description doesn't establish the boundary.

scenario: You have an agent that must always call at least one tool before responding. You want to prevent Claude from responding with plain text without making a tool call.
question: Which tool_choice setting enforces this?
options: tool_choice: { type: 'auto' } — Claude decides whether to use a tool
tool_choice: { type: 'tool', name: 'specific_tool' } — forces a specific tool call
tool_choice: { type: 'any' } — Claude must call one of the available tools
Remove tool_choice from the request — Claude will always use tools if available
explanation: tool_choice: { type: 'any' } forces Claude to call at least one tool from the available set, but gives it freedom to choose which one. tool_choice: auto (A) is the default — Claude may respond with plain text if it judges no tool is needed. Forcing a specific tool (B) would work only if there's exactly one appropriate tool. Omitting tool_choice (D) defaults to auto. The three modes: auto (Claude decides), any (must call a tool, Claude picks), specific tool (must call that exact tool). Platform note: Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Fable 5.1 reject forced tool_choice ('any' or a named tool) with a 400 error; on those models use 'auto' with strict tool use, or structured outputs.

scenario: A single customer service agent has 25 tools covering account management, billing, shipping, returns, and technical support. The descriptions are already detailed and clearly differentiated, yet logs show Claude still picks a tool from the wrong area for about one request in five.
question: What architectural change will most improve tool selection accuracy?
options: Add few-shot examples for every tool to the system prompt
Lengthen the system prompt to restate each tool's purpose
Give a coordinator a small routing tool set and delegate to specialized subagents that hold only their own area's tools
Raise the temperature so Claude explores more tool options
explanation: C is correct: once descriptions are already good, the remaining problem is the size of the decision. The exam guide's principle is that too many tools on one agent (its example: 18 instead of 4-5) degrades selection reliability, and the fix is scoped tool distribution, so each specialized subagent chooses among its own handful of tools while the coordinator routes. A is wrong because examples help with ambiguous cases but don't shrink the choice set, and they add prompt tokens. B is wrong because restating what the tool descriptions already say adds context without new information. D is wrong because temperature adds randomness and does nothing for selection accuracy. Anthropic's tool docs suggest related levers: consolidate overlapping operations, namespace tool names, and use tool search to load tools on demand.

scenario: A tool call to your external API fails with a 503 Service Unavailable error. Your tool needs to return a result to Claude.
question: What is the correct tool_result structure for this failure?
options: Return an empty tool_result and let Claude infer something went wrong
Throw an exception in the tool handler to abort the conversation
Return a tool_result with is_error: true and a structured content block containing the error type, message, and retryable: true
Return a tool_result with the error as plain text: '503 error occurred'
explanation: The correct pattern is a structured tool_result with is_error: true and a content block that includes: error type (503/service_unavailable), human-readable message, and a retryable flag. The retryable: true field is critical — it tells Claude (and the coordinator) that this is a transient failure that can be retried, not a permanent one. An empty result (A) causes Claude to proceed with bad assumptions. Exceptions (B) crash the loop. Plain text errors (D) require Claude to parse the error, which is fragile.

scenario: You are designing an MCP server for a file management system. Some operations need to be performed (write_file, delete_file) while others are informational (list_files, get_file_metadata).
question: How should you differentiate these in MCP server design?
options: Implement all of them as tools — tools are the universal MCP primitive
Use prompts for list_files and tools for write_file and delete_file
Implement all as resources with a read_only: true flag on informational ones
Implement write_file and delete_file as tools (actions that change state), and list_files / get_file_metadata as resources (read-only data access)
explanation: MCP has three primitives with distinct purposes: Tools = actions that execute code and change state (write, delete, send); Resources = read-only data access (metadata, catalogs, listings); Prompts = reusable prompt templates. Using resources for reads and tools for writes is the correct semantic split. It also enables clients to understand that resource calls are safe/read-only while tool calls may have side effects. Implementing everything as tools (A) works but loses semantic clarity and safety guarantees.

scenario: You need Claude to query two independent data sources in one turn: one to get customer data and another to get order history. These queries have no dependency on each other.
question: What is the most efficient implementation?
options: Submit both tool calls in the same assistant turn as parallel tool calls, then collect both results in one user turn
Sequential: query customer data first, then query order history in the next turn
Combine both queries into a single tool that accepts both IDs
Use streaming to interleave the two queries
explanation: Parallel tool calls — submitting multiple tool_use blocks in a single assistant turn — is exactly designed for independent operations. Claude sends both requests simultaneously, you execute them in parallel, and return both tool_results in a single user turn. This halves the round-trip latency vs. sequential. A combined tool (C) is a valid approach but tightly couples two concerns and is less flexible. Streaming (D) reduces time-to-first-token but doesn't parallelize execution. Sequential (B) wastes time when there's no dependency.

scenario: You are defining the JSON Schema for a tool parameter 'status' that can be: 'pending', 'active', 'suspended', or occasionally a custom string value the system doesn't yet know about.
question: How should you define this parameter in the schema?
options: type: 'string' with no constraints — accept anything
enum: ['pending', 'active', 'suspended'] — strict enum, reject unknowns
enum: ['pending', 'active', 'suspended', 'other'] with an additional 'custom_status' string field for when 'other' is selected
type: 'integer' mapping statuses to numbers for efficiency
explanation: The 'other' escape pattern is the correct schema design for enums that may need to accommodate unknown values. Define the known values as enum entries, add 'other' as an escape hatch, and provide a companion string field for the custom value. This preserves type safety for known values while gracefully handling the long tail. Unconstrained string (A) loses all type safety. Strict enum without 'other' (B) breaks for unexpected values — and unknown values will occur. Integer mappings (D) are opaque and maintenance-heavy.

scenario: You are building an MCP server with a tools catalog. When Claude needs to browse available operations before deciding which one to call, what MCP primitive is best suited for exposing the catalog?
question: Which MCP primitive should expose the operations catalog?
options: A tool called list_available_operations
A prompt template that lists all operations
A resource — resources are designed for metadata and catalog reads before actions are taken
Embed the catalog in every tool description
explanation: MCP Resources are specifically designed for read-only data that informs decision-making — exactly what a catalog is. Claude can read the resource to understand what's available before deciding which tool to call. This is the 'resources for metadata reads before actions' pattern. A tool (A) would work but is semantically wrong — tools are for actions with side effects. Prompt templates (B) are for reusable prompt patterns, not dynamic catalogs. Embedding in every description (D) bloats the tool context unnecessarily.

scenario: You need to ensure that whenever Claude calls a tool, the input always includes required fields and never includes unexpected fields.
question: What JSON Schema configuration enforces this?
options: Mark all fields as optional and validate server-side
Validate inputs in a PreToolUse hook and return an error if invalid
Add descriptions to each field explaining they are required
Set strict: true on the tool, list the required fields, and set additionalProperties: false
explanation: D is correct: strict: true turns on strict tool use, which guarantees Claude's tool inputs validate against your input_schema, so every field in the required array is present and types match; additionalProperties: false (required for strict schemas) rules out undeclared fields. C is wrong because descriptions are guidance, not constraints. B is wrong because a hook can reject bad input after the fact, but the schema prevents it from being generated in the first place. A is wrong because making everything optional removes the guarantee you want.

scenario: An MCP server has grown to 22 tools over time. You notice Claude is making incorrect tool selections in 30% of cases. You cannot reduce the number of features.
question: What is the correct architectural fix?
options: Rewrite all tool descriptions to be shorter and more concise
Increase the system prompt token budget to explain each tool more thoroughly
Split the 22 tools into 3-4 focused MCP servers (5-8 tools each), and route to the appropriate server based on the request domain
Use tool_choice: auto and trust Claude to improve with a better system prompt
explanation: C is correct: when every feature must stay and tool count is the problem, distributing tools across focused servers or agents keeps each request's choice small; the exam guide's principle is that too many tools on one agent (18 instead of 4-5 in its example) degrades selection. There is no documented exact threshold; the risk rises with count and overlap. A is wrong because shorter descriptions remove the differentiating detail that Anthropic's tool docs call the most important factor in tool performance. B is wrong because restating tools in the system prompt doesn't reduce the choice. D is wrong because 'auto' is already the default and a prompt cannot remove the decision load. Tool search (deferred loading) is another documented way to keep a large library out of context until it is needed.

scenario: Your agent has 25 tools available. During testing, you notice Claude frequently selects the wrong tool or fails to use tools when it should, especially for similar-sounding tools.
question: What is the primary cause and recommended fix according to Anthropic's best practices?
options: Large, overlapping tool sets make selection harder; shrink each agent's active set by scoping tools to roles, consolidating related operations, or loading tools on demand
Claude has a bug with large tool sets — file a support ticket and wait for a fix
Add 'IMPORTANT: always use tools when available' to the system prompt to force usage
Increase max_tokens to give Claude more space to reason about tool selection
explanation: A is correct: Anthropic's tool-use guidance is to keep the tool surface easy to navigate: write detailed descriptions, consolidate related operations into fewer tools, namespace tool names, and use tool search so large libraries load on demand. The exam guide adds that agents with too many tools (18 instead of 4-5 in its example) select less reliably. It is a decision-complexity effect with no fixed published cut-off, not a bug. B is wrong because nothing is broken that a ticket would fix. C is wrong because an emphatic prompt doesn't help Claude pick the right tool and can trigger unnecessary calls. D is wrong because max_tokens caps output length and has no bearing on tool choice.

scenario: Compliance needs every interaction logged. A teammate proposes setting tool_choice to {type: 'tool', name: 'log_interaction'} on every request so Claude 'always' logs.
question: What is the best way to meet the logging requirement?
options: Adopt the proposal: forcing log_interaction on every request guarantees the log
Use tool_choice: {type: 'any'} so Claude calls some tool on every turn
Log from your application code or a hook around each request and tool call, so logging never depends on the model
Tell Claude in the system prompt to call log_interaction at the end of every reply
explanation: C is correct: logging is a must-happen, deterministic requirement, so it belongs in code you control (your agent loop, or PreToolUse/PostToolUse hooks in Claude Code or the Agent SDK), not in a model decision. A is wrong because forcing a named tool makes that tool call the response itself: the model emits the tool_use block instead of answering and skips thinking, and Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Fable 5.1 reject forced tool_choice with a 400 error. B is wrong because 'any' only guarantees that some tool is called, not log_interaction. D is wrong because a prompt instruction is probabilistic and will sometimes be skipped.

scenario: You're designing a tool that queries a flaky external API. Sometimes the API returns timeout errors. You want Claude to handle this gracefully without stopping the conversation.
question: What is the recommended pattern for returning tool execution failures to Claude?
options: Return an error message to the user and ask them to retry the entire conversation
Throw an unhandled exception to terminate the agentic loop immediately
Catch the error silently and return an empty result so Claude doesn't worry about it
Return a tool_result with is_error: true and a descriptive error message, allowing Claude to adapt its approach
explanation: Returning is_error: true with a descriptive message lets Claude reason about the failure and decide next steps (retry, use alternative, or inform user gracefully). Asking users to retry breaks flow entirely. Silent empty results mislead Claude into thinking the tool returned nothing. Throwing exceptions prevents graceful degradation.

scenario: You need to expose a local SQLite database and a file system to Claude via MCP. You want to understand the protocol's capability model.
question: What are the three core MCP primitives that a server can expose to clients?
options: Tools (model-initiated actions), Resources (app-loaded read-only data), and Prompts (user-selected templates)
Functions, Variables, and Events
Endpoints, Schemas, and Hooks
Commands, Queries, and Subscriptions
explanation: MCP defines three primitives: Tools (callable functions the model decides to invoke), Resources (read-only data the application loads into context), and Prompts (reusable templates the user explicitly selects). The other options use terminology from other protocols — GraphQL (subscriptions), REST (endpoints), event systems — that don't apply to MCP's design.

scenario: You want to quickly prototype an MCP server in Python that exposes a 'get_weather' tool. You need the simplest possible implementation with minimal boilerplate.
question: Which framework provides the most concise way to create an MCP server with tool registration?
options: Write a raw JSON-RPC server from scratch with socket handling and protocol implementation
Use Flask with a custom MCP middleware adapter layer
Use FastMCP which provides decorator-based tool registration like @mcp.tool() for rapid MCP server development
Use the anthropic Python SDK's built-in MCP server class
explanation: FastMCP provides a high-level Python framework with decorator-based tool registration (@mcp.tool()), making MCP server creation as simple as writing a decorated function. Raw JSON-RPC requires implementing the full protocol manually. Flask isn't MCP-aware. The anthropic SDK is an API client library for calling Claude, not an MCP server framework.

scenario: Production logs show your customer support agent frequently calls get_customer when users ask about orders (e.g., 'check my order #12345'), instead of calling lookup_order. Both tools have minimal descriptions ('Retrieves customer information' / 'Retrieves order details') and accept similar identifier formats.
question: What's the most effective first step to improve tool selection reliability?
options: Add few-shot examples to the system prompt demonstrating correct tool selection patterns, with 5–8 examples showing order-related queries routing to lookup_order
Consolidate both tools into a single lookup_entity tool that accepts any identifier and internally determines which backend to query
Implement a routing layer that parses user input before each turn and pre-selects the appropriate tool based on detected keywords and identifier patterns
Expand each tool's description to include input formats it handles, example queries, edge cases, and boundaries explaining when to use it versus similar tools
explanation: Tool descriptions are the primary mechanism LLMs use for tool selection. When descriptions are minimal, models lack the context to differentiate between similar tools. Option D directly addresses this root cause with a low-effort, high-leverage fix. Few-shot examples (A) add token overhead without fixing the underlying issue of ambiguous descriptions. A routing layer (C) is over-engineered and bypasses the LLM's natural language understanding. Consolidating tools (B) is a valid architectural choice but requires more effort than a 'first step' warrants.

scenario: Your synthesis agent currently routes all claim verifications through the coordinator → web search agent → re-invoke synthesis. This adds 2–3 round trips per task and increases latency by 40%. Evaluation shows 85% of verifications are simple fact-checks (dates, names, statistics) while 15% require deeper investigation.
question: What is the most effective approach to reduce overhead while maintaining system reliability?
options: Give the synthesis agent a scoped verify_fact tool for simple lookups, while complex verifications continue delegating to the web search agent through the coordinator
Have the synthesis agent accumulate all verification needs and return them as a batch to the coordinator at the end of its pass, which then sends them all to the web search agent at once
Give the synthesis agent access to all web search tools so it can handle any verification need directly without round-trips through the coordinator
Have the web search agent proactively cache extra context around each source during initial research, anticipating what the synthesis agent might need to verify
explanation: Option A applies the principle of least privilege by giving the synthesis agent only what it needs for the 85% common case (simple fact verification) while preserving the existing coordination pattern for complex cases. Option B's batching approach creates blocking dependencies since synthesis steps may depend on earlier verified facts. Option C over-provisions the synthesis agent, violating separation of concerns and degrading tool selection reliability. Option D relies on speculative caching that cannot reliably predict what the synthesis agent will need to verify.

scenario: A generic analyze_document tool is used for extraction, summarization, and claim verification, and results are inconsistent.
question: Which refactor improves reliability?
options: Split it into purpose-specific tools (extract_data_points, summarize_content, verify_claim_against_source) with defined input/output contracts
Add more text to the single tool's description
Remove the tool entirely
Route all three uses through Grep
explanation: Splitting an overloaded generic tool into purpose-specific tools with clear contracts improves selection and result quality. More description text (B) doesn't resolve the overload, removing it (C) loses capability, and Grep (D) can't perform these semantic operations.

scenario: A well-written tool description exists, but a keyword-sensitive line in the system prompt keeps steering Claude to the wrong tool.
question: What should you review?
options: Only the tool description
The model temperature
The system prompt for keyword-sensitive instructions that create unintended tool associations overriding good descriptions
The user's phrasing only
explanation: System-prompt wording can create keyword associations that override even good tool descriptions, so review it for such triggers. Focusing only on the description (A), temperature (B), or user phrasing (D) misses the actual cause in the system prompt.

scenario: An MCP tool fails and returns a generic 'Operation failed' message, so the agent can't decide what to do next.
question: What is the recommended error-response design?
options: Keep the generic message; less detail is safer
Throw an unstructured exception
Return an empty success
Return structured metadata: errorCategory (transient/validation/business/permission), isRetryable boolean, and a human-readable description
explanation: Structured error metadata (errorCategory, isRetryable, human-readable description) lets the agent choose the right recovery. Generic messages (A) block informed decisions, empty success (C) hides failures, and unstructured exceptions (B) crash the loop.

scenario: Your MCP tool blocked an action due to a business-rule violation (over-limit refund).
question: How should the error be represented so the agent responds appropriately?
options: A business-category error with retriable: false and a customer-friendly explanation so the agent communicates rather than retries
isRetryable: true with a generic message
A transient error so the agent retries
No error; silently succeed
explanation: Business-rule violations are non-retryable; marking retriable: false with a clear explanation lets the agent communicate the outcome instead of pointlessly retrying. Marking it retryable/transient (B, C) causes wasted retries, and silent success (D) violates the rule.

scenario: The MCP isError flag is central to failure handling.
question: What is its role?
options: It formats successful output
It caches results
It signals to the agent that a tool call failed, so failures are communicated back distinctly from successful results
It sets tool_choice
explanation: The isError flag communicates tool failures back to the agent, distinguishing errors from successful results. It doesn't format success (A), cache (B), or configure tool_choice (D).

scenario: A subagent distinguishes between 'could not access the service' and 'query succeeded but returned no rows.'
question: Why does this distinction matter for error handling?
options: It doesn't; both should be retried
Empty results should always raise exceptions
Both should be treated as fatal
Access failures may warrant retry decisions, while valid empty results are successful and should not trigger retries
explanation: Access failures may need retries, but a valid empty result is a successful query with no matches and shouldn't be retried. Treating both as retryable (A) or fatal (C) is wrong, and raising exceptions on empty results (B) misrepresents success.

scenario: An agent has been given 18 tools and its tool selection has become unreliable.
question: What does this illustrate and how do you fix it?
options: Too many tools degrade selection reliability; scope each agent to the 4-5 tools it actually needs
More tools always improve capability; keep all 18
Reduce max_tokens
Set tool_choice to 'any'
explanation: Giving an agent too many tools (e.g., 18) increases decision complexity and degrades selection; scoping to the ~4-5 relevant tools restores reliability. More tools aren't always better (B), and max_tokens (C) or tool_choice (D) don't address selection overload.

scenario: A synthesis agent that shouldn't search the web has been given web-search tools and keeps misusing them.
question: What principle guides the fix?
options: Give every agent every tool for flexibility
Increase temperature so it self-corrects
Scope tool access to each agent's role; remove tools outside its specialization to prevent misuse
Add a second synthesis agent
explanation: Agents with tools outside their specialization tend to misuse them; scoping tools to role prevents this. Universal tool access (A) causes exactly this problem, temperature (B) doesn't fix scope, and adding agents (D) doesn't remove the misused tools.

scenario: A generic fetch_url tool is being used to load documents and sometimes fetches invalid or unintended URLs.
question: Which replacement improves safety and reliability?
options: Keep fetch_url but add a prompt warning
Give the agent Bash to curl URLs
Remove URL loading entirely
Replace it with a constrained load_document tool that validates document URLs
explanation: Replacing a broad tool with a constrained alternative (load_document that validates URLs) reduces misuse while preserving the needed capability. A prompt warning (A) is probabilistic, removing loading (C) breaks the feature, and Bash/curl (B) widens the attack surface.

scenario: You want to guarantee the model calls a tool rather than replying with conversational text, though it may choose which tool.
question: Which tool_choice setting applies?
options: tool_choice: 'any'
tool_choice: 'auto'
tool_choice: 'none'
tool_choice: {"type":"tool","name":"x"}
explanation: tool_choice: 'any' forces a tool call while leaving the choice to the model. 'auto' (B) permits text, 'none' (C) forbids tools, and forcing a named tool (D) removes choice. Platform note: Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Fable 5.1 reject forced tool_choice ('any' or a named tool) with a 400 error; on those models use 'auto' with strict tool use, or structured outputs.

scenario: You want a shared MCP server available to the whole team with credentials injected without committing secrets.
question: How do you configure it?
options: Hard-code the token in .mcp.json and commit it
Put it in ~/.claude.json so only you have it
Configure the server in project-scoped .mcp.json using environment variable expansion (e.g., ${GITHUB_TOKEN}) for the credential
Store the token in CLAUDE.md
explanation: Project-scoped .mcp.json with env-var expansion (${GITHUB_TOKEN}) shares the server team-wide while keeping secrets out of version control. Hard-coding secrets (A) leaks them, user scope (B) doesn't share with the team, and CLAUDE.md (D) is not for credentials.

scenario: You are experimenting with a personal MCP server you don't want to impose on teammates.
question: Where should it be configured?
options: Project-scoped .mcp.json committed to the repo
In the root CLAUDE.md
In every teammate's shell profile
User-scoped ~/.claude.json for personal/experimental servers
explanation: Personal/experimental MCP servers belong in user-scoped ~/.claude.json so they don't affect the team. Project .mcp.json (A) would share them, teammates' profiles (C) is intrusive, and CLAUDE.md (B) is not an MCP config location.

scenario: You configure two MCP servers simultaneously and wonder whether the agent can use tools from both.
question: What is true about tool discovery across servers?
options: Tools from all configured MCP servers are discovered at connection time and available simultaneously
Only the first server's tools are available
You must manually enable each tool per turn
Servers are mutually exclusive
explanation: All configured MCP servers have their tools discovered at connection time and available to the agent simultaneously. It isn't limited to the first server (B), doesn't require per-turn enabling (C), and servers aren't mutually exclusive (D).

scenario: Your agent keeps preferring built-in Grep over a more capable MCP tool that could answer directly.
question: How do you encourage correct selection of the MCP tool?
options: Delete the Grep tool
Lower temperature
Enhance the MCP tool's description to clearly explain its capabilities and outputs so the agent prefers it when appropriate
Force tool_choice to Grep
explanation: Improving the MCP tool's description to detail its capabilities/outputs helps the agent prefer it over built-ins like Grep when appropriate. Deleting Grep (A) removes a useful tool, temperature (B) doesn't change selection logic, and forcing Grep (D) is the opposite of the goal.

scenario: You need a standard integration with Jira and are deciding between building a custom MCP server or using an existing community one.
question: What is the recommended approach?
options: Always build custom servers for full control
Use Bash to call Jira's API directly
Never use MCP for third-party tools
Prefer existing community MCP servers for standard integrations; reserve custom servers for team-specific workflows
explanation: For standard integrations like Jira, prefer existing community MCP servers and reserve custom builds for genuinely team-specific needs. Always-custom (A) wastes effort, avoiding MCP (C) forgoes its benefits, and raw Bash API calls (B) bypass structured tooling.

scenario: Your agents make many exploratory tool calls just to discover what data exists (issue lists, doc hierarchies, schemas).
question: Which MCP capability reduces these exploratory calls?
options: MCP resources that expose content catalogs so agents can see available data without exploratory tool calls
More tools
Higher max_tokens
tool_choice: 'any'
explanation: MCP resources expose content catalogs (issue summaries, doc hierarchies, schemas), giving agents visibility into available data and reducing exploratory tool calls. Adding tools (B) or tokens (C) doesn't provide a catalog, and tool_choice (D) doesn't expose data.

scenario: You are deciding whether to model a capability as an MCP tool or an MCP resource.
question: Which mapping is correct?
options: Use tools for content catalogs and resources for actions
Tools and resources are interchangeable
Use resources for content catalogs (browsable data) and tools for actions (operations the agent performs)
Always use tools; resources are deprecated
explanation: Resources expose browsable content catalogs, while tools perform actions/operations. Option A inverts this. They aren't interchangeable (B), and resources are a first-class MCP concept, not deprecated (D).

scenario: You need to search file contents across a codebase for all callers of a function.
question: Which built-in tool is appropriate?
options: Glob
Edit
Write
Grep
explanation: Grep searches file contents for patterns (like function names/callers), making it the right tool here. Glob (A) matches file paths by name/extension, and Write/Edit (C, B) modify files rather than search content.

scenario: You need to find all files matching a naming pattern like **/*.test.tsx.
question: Which built-in tool is appropriate?
options: Glob
Grep
Bash cat
Read
explanation: Glob matches file paths by name/extension patterns (**/*.test.tsx). Grep (B) searches contents, cat (C) prints a file, and Read (D) loads a specific file's contents - none of which enumerate files by pattern.

scenario: You try to modify a file with Edit, but the anchor text appears multiple times and Edit can't uniquely match it.
question: What is the recommended fallback?
options: Give up on the change
Use Grep to overwrite the file
Use Read to load the full file, then Write the updated contents
Use Glob to modify the file
explanation: C is correct: when Edit can't find a unique anchor, reading the full file and writing back the modified contents is a reliable fallback. Edit itself also accepts a longer old_string with enough surrounding context to pin down one occurrence, or replace_all: true when every occurrence should change. A is wrong because the change is still achievable. B and D are wrong because Grep and Glob search; they don't modify files.

scenario: You are exploring a large unfamiliar codebase and want to build understanding without reading everything upfront.
question: Which incremental strategy is recommended?
options: Read every file first, then reason
Use Bash to print the whole repo
Glob all files and load them into context
Start with Grep to find entry points, then Read to follow imports and trace flows incrementally
explanation: Incremental understanding - Grep for entry points, then Read to follow imports and trace flows - avoids context exhaustion and builds a targeted mental model. Reading everything (A), loading all files (C), or dumping the repo (B) floods context and wastes budget.

scenario: You must trace how a function is used across wrapper modules that re-export it under different names.
question: Which approach works?
options: First identify all exported names, then Grep for each name across the codebase to trace usage
Read one file and assume it's the only usage
Glob for the function's file only
Rely on the model's memory of the code
explanation: Tracing usage through wrappers requires identifying all exported names, then Grepping each across the codebase. Reading one file (B) misses re-exports, Glob for one file (C) doesn't trace usage, and relying on memory (D) is unreliable for specific code.

scenario: A synthesis agent occasionally needs simple fact verification, but full web tools would over-provision it.
question: How do you balance capability and least privilege?
options: Give it all web tools
Give it no verification ability
Provide a scoped verify_fact tool for high-frequency simple lookups while routing complex verifications through the coordinator
Set tool_choice: 'none'
explanation: A scoped cross-role tool (verify_fact) covers the common simple case without over-provisioning, while complex cases route through the coordinator. Full web tools (A) violate least privilege, no verification (B) breaks the need, and 'none' (D) disables tools.

scenario: You want to force extract_metadata to run before enrichment tools within a tool-using agent.
question: Which tool_choice configuration guarantees the first call?
options: tool_choice: 'auto'
tool_choice: 'none'
tool_choice: 'any'
tool_choice: {"type":"tool","name":"extract_metadata"}
explanation: Forcing the named tool (extract_metadata) guarantees it runs first; later steps proceed in follow-up turns. 'auto' (A) may return text, 'any' (C) may call a different tool, and 'none' (B) forbids tools. Platform note: Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Fable 5.1 reject forced tool_choice ('any' or a named tool) with a 400 error; on those models use 'auto' with strict tool use, or structured outputs.

scenario: An MCP tool experiences a timeout talking to a backend service.
question: Which errorCategory best fits, and what should isRetryable be?
options: transient; isRetryable true
validation; isRetryable false
business; isRetryable false
permission; isRetryable false
explanation: A backend timeout is a transient error and is typically retryable, so category 'transient' with isRetryable true is appropriate. Validation (B) and business (C) errors are input/policy issues (non-retryable), and permission (D) requires access changes, not a retry.

scenario: Your team gives a coordinator many cross-role tools 'just in case,' and selection quality drops.
question: Which distribution strategy is better?
options: Maximize tools on the coordinator
Put all tools on every subagent
Scope tools per role with only limited cross-role tools for specific high-frequency needs
Remove all tools from subagents
explanation: Scoping tools per role, with only a few cross-role tools for genuine high-frequency needs, preserves selection quality. Maximizing tools (A) or putting all tools everywhere (B) degrades selection, and removing all subagent tools (D) breaks their function.

scenario: You must decide when to consolidate two tools into one versus keep them separate.
question: Which guidance is soundest?
options: Always consolidate to reduce count
Tool boundaries don't affect selection
Always split every tool as finely as possible
Split when responsibilities/contracts differ enough to cause ambiguity; consolidate only when they truly share one clear purpose
explanation: Boundaries should follow clear, distinct contracts: split when consolidation causes ambiguity, consolidate only when there's a single clear purpose. Always-consolidate (A) reintroduces overload, always-split (C) creates needless fragmentation, and boundaries clearly affect selection (B).

scenario: A tool description omits input format details, so the agent frequently passes malformed inputs.
question: What is the fix?
options: Include input formats, example queries, and edge cases in the tool description so the agent supplies correct inputs
Add retries around the tool
Lower temperature
Force the tool with tool_choice
explanation: Documenting input formats, example queries, and edge cases in the description helps the agent supply correct inputs. Retries (B) don't teach correct inputs, temperature (C) doesn't fix format knowledge, and forcing the tool (D) doesn't ensure valid arguments.

scenario: A developer runs claude mcp add --transport http jira https://mcp.example.com/jira with no scope flag and tells the team the Jira server is 'set up for everyone'.
question: What did the command actually do?
options: Added the server at local scope (the default) in ~/.claude.json, for this user and project only; --scope project writes .mcp.json for the team
Added the server to the project's .mcp.json, so teammates get it on their next pull
Added the server at user scope, so every developer on the team can use it
Added the server to .claude/settings.json, which is shared through the repository
explanation: A is correct: the Claude Code MCP docs define three scopes: local (the default, stored in ~/.claude.json, current project only, not shared), project (.mcp.json in the repo root, shared through version control), and user (~/.claude.json, all of your own projects). Sharing with the team takes --scope project and a commit. B is wrong because that only happens with --scope project. C is wrong because user scope is still personal: it spans your projects, not your teammates. D is wrong because claude mcp add writes to ~/.claude.json or .mcp.json depending on scope, not to .claude/settings.json.
